proposals.title: 3D printing station
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

Hardware projects at the hub stall at the same point: the firmware works, the board works, and the case never gets made. Ordering prints online costs days and money for parts that should take an hour. A printer in the space turns "I'll print it at some point" into "I printed it tonight".

A shared printer also brings people in. Prints are visible, tangible and easy to talk about, and a printing corner is a natural first task for a new member who does not yet write Solidity.

## What we will buy

- One enclosed CoreXY printer with auto bed levelling (Bambu Lab P1S class), spare nozzles and build plates
- A starter stock of PLA and PETG, plus one roll of TPU, in the hub's colours
- A lockable cabinet for filament with silica gel, tools, deburring knives and calipers
- A dedicated shelf with a small fume filter and a fire-safe base

## Rules of use

- The printer is free for members; guests pay filament at cost
- Prints are queued on the hub board, longest jobs run overnight
- Two members act as maintainers; they run the calibration print each month

## Milestones

### A - Printer running - 1,100 EURC

- [ ] Printer, plates, nozzles and filament stock bought and installed on a dedicated shelf
- [ ] Calibration print and a first hub-branded print published in the hub chat
- [ ] Cabinet, tools and safety base in place

### B - Onboarding - 300 EURC

- [ ] One evening workshop: design a part in a free CAD tool, slice it, print it, with at least 10 attendees
- [ ] A one-page guide on the hub wiki: how to queue, slice, load filament, and who to call when it clogs
- [ ] Two named maintainers and a monthly maintenance checklist

proposals.title: Urbe Hub anniversary party
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

A community that never celebrates burns out. A party is where members bring friends, where people who left come back, and where the hub gets the photos and the stories it needs to recruit next year. The demo table and talks keep it about what people built.

## What we will do

- Rent tables, sound and lighting for one evening at the hub or a nearby venue
- Food and drinks for 100 people, with a vegetarian and vegan option
- A DJ or a member playlist and a small stage for five 5-minute talks
- A demo table of projects built at the hub during the year
- A photographer and a 2-minute recap video

## Milestones

### A - Preparation - 800 EURC

- [ ] Date, venue, talk line-up and demo list published at least 3 weeks before
- [ ] Deposits paid for sound, food and venue

### B - The party - 2,000 EURC

- [ ] Event held with at least 80 attendees, talks and demos as planned
- [ ] Photos and the recap video published within 2 weeks, and the expense sheet posted

proposals.title: Cooling for summer
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

The space is at its best in spring and autumn and nearly empty in summer, exactly when students and remote workers have the most free time. One split unit or two good portable units keep the room at a working temperature and keep the machines from overheating.

## What we will buy

- One split air conditioner (12,000 BTU class) installed by a licensed technician, subject to the landlord's approval, or
- Two portable units with window kits if a split cannot be installed
- A ceiling fan for the small room and blackout blinds for the sun-facing windows

## Milestones

### A - Installed - 2,000 EURC

- [ ] Landlord approval obtained, unit installed and tested, invoice published
- [ ] Blinds and ceiling fan installed

### B - Running - 300 EURC

- [ ] First summer's electricity increase covered from this milestone and reported
- [ ] Attendance in July and August compared with the previous year, published

proposals.title: Electronics bench
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

Members bring hardware wallets, dev boards and sensor projects to the hub and end up soldering on the kitchen table with a borrowed iron. There is no way to measure a signal, no stable power supply, and no stock of the resistors and headers every board needs. A bench costs less than a laptop and unlocks a whole class of projects.

## What we will buy

- Soldering station with temperature control and a hot-air rework station
- Bench power supply (30 V, 5 A, current limited)
- Entry-level 2-channel oscilloscope and a logic analyser
- Two multimeters, a magnifier lamp, helping hands, fume extractor
- Component drawers stocked with resistors, capacitors, headers, jumper wires, common ICs, USB cables, and an ESP32 and RP2040 board each
- ESD mat and wrist straps

## Milestones

### A - Bench built - 900 EURC

- [ ] All equipment bought, bench assembled, ESD mat and extractor installed
- [ ] Component drawers labelled and an inventory sheet on the hub wiki

### B - First workshop - 200 EURC

- [ ] One "solder your first board" evening with kits for at least 12 people
- [ ] A bench guide on the wiki: safety, how to use the scope, how to restock

proposals.title: Ergonomic seating and desks
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

People stay in a space where they can sit for eight hours. The current mix of donated chairs and folding tables is fine for an evening meetup and painful for a work day, which is exactly the use that makes a hackerspace a home base rather than an event venue.

## What we will buy

- 10 task chairs with adjustable height, lumbar support and armrests
- 2 electric height-adjustable desks
- 6 monitor arms and 4 used 27-inch monitors
- Power strips with USB-C PD at every desk, and cable trays

## Milestones

### A - Chairs and desks - 2,900 EURC

- [ ] Chairs and desks bought and assembled, old chairs donated or recycled
- [ ] Photo of the new layout published with a floor plan on the wiki

### B - Desk setup - 700 EURC

- [ ] Monitors, arms, power and cable trays installed at every desk
- [ ] A short survey of members after one month, published with what changed

proposals.title: Focus and call room
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

Every day someone takes a call in the main room and everyone else goes quiet, or the caller steps into the corridor. A treated room with decent audio lets the hub host remote meetings, record talks and interviews, and gives members a quiet place when the main room is loud.

## What we will buy

- Acoustic panels for the walls and ceiling, a rug, and a door sweep and seal
- A USB microphone, a 1080p webcam, a key light and a small monitor
- A desk, two chairs and a whiteboard
- A door sign and a shared booking calendar

## Milestones

### A - Room treated - 1,200 EURC

- [ ] Panels, rug and door seal installed, before and after noise measurement published
- [ ] Desk, chairs and whiteboard in place

### B - Call setup - 600 EURC

- [ ] Microphone, camera, light and monitor installed and a test recording published
- [ ] Booking calendar live and linked from the wiki, with the house rules on the door

proposals.title: Hub node rack
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

An Ethereum hackerspace should run Ethereum. A node in the room gives members a local RPC that never rate-limits, a validator that the whole community can watch and learn from, and a hands-on way to teach what a client actually does. A home server next to it hosts the things a space needs and nobody wants to pay a cloud bill for.

## What we will buy

- A fanless or low-noise mini PC (8-core, 64 GB RAM, 4 TB NVMe) for the execution and consensus clients
- A second small server (32 GB RAM, 2 TB SSD) for the wiki, a CI runner, a file share and a Home Assistant instance
- A small rack or shelf, a managed switch, a UPS, and cable management
- One year of a fixed IP or a tunnel for the public endpoint

The validator stake is not part of this proposal; the hub deposits it separately or joins a pooled staking setup.

## Milestones

### A - Node online - 1,700 EURC

- [ ] Hardware bought and racked, execution and consensus clients synced on mainnet
- [ ] Local RPC reachable on the hub network, documented on the wiki
- [ ] Monitoring dashboard on a screen in the space showing sync, peers and the validator

### B - Shared services - 600 EURC

- [ ] Second server running the wiki, a CI runner and a file share with backups
- [ ] One "run your own node" workshop, at least 10 attendees
- [ ] A rota of two members responsible for updates, listed on the wiki

proposals.title: Kitchen corner
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

A kitchen is where a hackerspace's conversations happen. Right now coffee means leaving the building, and meetup snacks arrive in plastic bags with nowhere to go. A working corner with a real espresso machine is the cheapest upgrade to how long people stay and how much they talk.

## What we will buy

- A bean-to-cup or semi-automatic espresso machine and a grinder
- A fridge with freezer compartment, a kettle, a microwave
- A water filter jug or under-sink filter
- Shelves, containers, a dish rack, mugs and glasses for 30 people
- A starter supply of beans, tea and snacks, and a jar for contributions

## Milestones

### A - Corner equipped - 1,200 EURC

- [ ] Appliances bought, installed and a cleaning rota on the wall
- [ ] Shelves, containers and mugs in place

### B - Supplies - 200 EURC

- [ ] First month of beans, tea and snacks bought and a contribution rule agreed and posted

proposals.title: Laser cutter
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

Half of what a hackerspace builds is flat: front panels, enclosures, stands, signs, badges, stencils. A laser cutter makes all of it in minutes from a vector file. Together with the 3D printer it closes the loop from idea to physical object without leaving the space, and it is the tool that most often gets a passer-by to sign up.

## What we will buy

- A desktop diode or small CO2 laser (400 x 400 mm bed class) with a safety enclosure
- Fume extractor with carbon filter and a window vent kit
- Honeycomb bed, air assist, fire blanket and CO2 extinguisher next to the machine
- A starter stock of 3 mm plywood, 3 mm acrylic and cardboard

## Rules of use

- Never left running unattended; a trained member is present for every job
- Materials list on the wall: what may be cut and what may not (no PVC, no unknown plastics)
- Two named operators train new users in a 30-minute session before their first job

## Milestones

### A - Machine installed - 2,600 EURC

- [ ] Cutter, enclosure, extractor, vent and safety kit installed and a test cut published
- [ ] Wall sign with allowed materials and the emergency procedure
- [ ] Two trained operators named on the wiki

### B - Materials and onboarding - 600 EURC

- [ ] Material stock bought and a restocking rule in place
- [ ] One workshop: design a box in a free vector tool and cut it, at least 10 attendees
- [ ] The hub's outdoor sign cut on the machine

proposals.title: Library and study corner
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

A hackerspace collects knowledge as well as tools. A small library gives students something to pick up while they wait for a build, gives members a quiet corner, and gives the space a memory. The books are chosen by the members and the shelf grows with donations.

## What we will buy

- Two bookshelves, two armchairs, a small table and two reading lamps
- About 40 books chosen by a member poll: cryptography, distributed systems, Ethereum, electronics, hardware design, and a few classics of hacker culture
- A sign-out sheet and bookplates

## Milestones

### A - Corner built - 350 EURC

- [ ] Shelves, chairs, lamps and table bought and set up, photo published

### B - Books - 400 EURC

- [ ] Member poll run, books bought and catalogued on the wiki with a sign-out sheet

proposals.title: Lighting, signage and mural
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

The room looks like an office at night and is invisible from the street. Lighting changes how long people stay, and a sign and a mural tell the neighbourhood that this is an open community space, not a closed company.

## What we will do

- Replace the tube lighting with dimmable warm LED panels and add desk lamps
- Cut an outdoor sign on the hub laser cutter or order one, with the hub name and opening hours
- Commission a mural from a Rome-based artist through an open call among members
- Add LED strips and a projector-friendly wall for events

## Milestones

### A - Lighting and sign - 900 EURC

- [ ] New lighting installed, before and after photos published
- [ ] Outdoor sign installed with opening hours and the hub's link

### B - Mural - 700 EURC

- [ ] Open call run, artist chosen by member vote, sketch approved
- [ ] Mural painted and unveiled at a hub evening, photos published

proposals.title: Open hardware member badge
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

A badge is the classic hackerspace project: it teaches PCB design, soldering and firmware, gives every member something they built themselves, and becomes the object people hand to visitors. Adding a small secure-element demo makes it a teaching tool for how a hardware wallet signs.

## What we will do

- Design a badge around an ESP32 or RP2040 with an e-paper or OLED display, a few buttons and a battery, in an open source CAD tool
- Produce 60 kits: PCBs, components, and a laser-cut or printed case from the hub's own machines
- Firmware with a name display, a hub schedule screen and a signing demo
- Publish schematics, layout, firmware and the assembly guide under an open hardware licence

## Milestones

### A - Design and prototype - 500 EURC

- [ ] Schematic and layout published, 5 prototypes assembled and photographed
- [ ] Firmware with the three screens running on a prototype

### B - Production and workshop - 900 EURC

- [ ] 60 kits produced and cased
- [ ] Assembly workshop held with at least 20 badges soldered and working
- [ ] Repository with the full design and assembly guide linked from the hub wiki

proposals.title: Visiting hacker residency
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

The fastest way to raise the level of a space is to bring in people who have built things elsewhere. A week is long enough to work together, not just to give a talk. In return the hub gets a talk, a written guide or a shared project, and a link to another community.

## What we will do

- Open call for residents, chosen by member vote; priority to people from other hackerspaces and Ethereum builder communities
- Each resident receives travel and 7 nights of accommodation in Rome, and a desk at the hub
- Each resident gives one public talk or workshop and writes a short post about the week
- Residents are spread over 6 months so the space always has one recent visit to talk about

## Milestones

### A - First resident - 950 EURC

- [ ] Open call run and three residents chosen and announced
- [ ] First residency completed with a public talk and a post

### B - Second resident - 950 EURC

- [ ] Second residency completed with a public talk and a post

### C - Third resident - 900 EURC

- [ ] Third residency completed with a public talk and a post
- [ ] A summary of the programme with what each visit left behind

proposals.title: Weekend hackathon
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

Hackathons are how the hub turns visitors into members and ideas into repositories. A small local edition, at the space, with mentors from the community, costs a fraction of a big event and produces projects that keep being worked on in the room where they started.

## What we will do

- Two days, Saturday morning to Sunday evening, at the hub
- Breakfast, lunch and dinner for 40 people on both days
- Four mentors with a stipend, covering Solidity, frontend, ZK and hardware
- Prizes: three small pools, decided by a member vote at the demo session
- Every project in a public repository under an open source licence

## Milestones

### A - Preparation - 600 EURC

- [ ] Date, theme, mentors and rules published at least 4 weeks before
- [ ] Registration open, with at least 30 sign-ups before the event

### B - The event - 3,000 EURC

- [ ] Event held with at least 30 participants and at least 8 projects demoed
- [ ] Prizes paid, all repositories linked from a public page, expense sheet posted

proposals.title: Workshop series
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

Members ask for the same things every month: how to write a contract, how a ZK circuit works, how to solder, how to keep keys safe. Regular workshops answer that at scale, give members a reason to come on a fixed evening, and give the hub a library of recordings.

## What we will do

- Six evenings, one per month, 2 hours each, at the hub
- Topics: Solidity from zero, a first ZK circuit, solder a board, model and print a part, personal opsec and key management, run an Ethereum node
- Each facilitator receives a stipend and a materials budget for kits
- Each session recorded and published with the slides and exercises

## Milestones

### A - First three sessions - 1,100 EURC

- [ ] Calendar and facilitators published for all six sessions
- [ ] Three sessions held with at least 12 attendees each, recordings and materials published

### B - Last three sessions - 1,100 EURC

- [ ] Three more sessions held with at least 12 attendees each, recordings and materials published
- [ ] Attendee feedback collected and a short report on what to repeat next year

proposals.title: Arkiv mainnet launch events
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

A mainnet launch is a one-time chance to get developers to try a product. Arkiv's launch lands around Devcon, when the community is already travelling and looking for things to build. Community-run events are cheaper than the foundation running them, reach local developer groups the foundation does not, and give the launch a presence in three cities instead of one conference hall.

The events are hands-on by design: the measure of success is how many people leave with something written to Arkiv, not how many chairs were filled.

## What we will do

- **Three city meetups** hosted by local communities: Urbe Hub in Rome, and partner communities in Warsaw and Lisbon. Each evening: a 20-minute talk on Arkiv, a 90-minute workshop where attendees write and query their first records, and lightning demos of what people built.
- **Devcon side event**: a half-day workshop track with three sessions (first records, agent memory with the MCP server, building a small app), open to Devcon attendees, with the reference apps as the material.
- Every talk recorded and published; every workshop published as a self-guided tutorial afterwards.

## Budget

- Venues, food and drinks for about 50 people per city meetup and 100 at the side event
- Travel for one facilitator between the three cities
- Workshop material and a small prize per event for the best demo
- Recording and editing

## Requirements

- Each event publishes attendee count and the number of wallets that wrote to Arkiv during the workshop
- Talks and workshops published within two weeks, under an open licence
- Expense sheet published after the last event

## Milestones

### A - City meetups - 9,000 USDC

- [ ] Three meetups held with at least 30 attendees each and at least 15 wallets writing to Arkiv in each workshop
- [ ] Recordings and self-guided tutorials published

### B - Devcon side event - 11,000 USDC

- [ ] Side event held with at least 60 attendees and three workshop sessions delivered
- [ ] Recordings published, expense sheet for all four events posted

proposals.title: Arkiv reference apps
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

Arkiv is where Golem's effort goes now: a new testnet this month, audits through October, and a mainnet around Devcon. Its pitch is "a database with blockchain guarantees", and the use cases on the site are leaderboards, agent memory and historical records. What is missing is a working app for each of those that a developer can clone, run and read in an hour. Docs describe an API; reference apps show what to build with it, and they catch the SDK's rough edges before mainnet users do.

The three apps are chosen to cover the three things Arkiv does differently from a normal database: wallet-owned rows, time-scoped storage that expires, and queries over indexed attributes.

## What we will build

- **Leaderboard**: a browser game where every score is a row owned by the player's wallet; scores expire after a season; the board is a query. Shows ownership and expiry.
- **Agent memory**: an assistant that stores its conversation memory on Arkiv through the Arkiv MCP server, so the memory is portable between agents and owned by the user. Shows the MCP path and per-user data.
- **DAO audit log**: proposals, votes and payouts of a small DAO written to Arkiv, with a page that reconstructs the history from queries alone. Shows tamper evidence and historical records.

Each app: one repository, a deployed demo on the testnet, a tutorial that builds it from an empty folder, and a list of SDK issues found while building it, filed upstream.

## Requirements

- Open source, each under 2,000 lines so it can be read in one sitting
- Built on the September testnet and re-verified on mainnet within 30 days of launch
- Every friction point found in the SDK or docs is filed as an issue with a reproduction

## Milestones

### A - Leaderboard - 6,000 USDC

- [ ] App deployed on testnet, repository and tutorial published
- [ ] SDK and docs issues filed

### B - Agent memory - 7,000 USDC

- [ ] App deployed on testnet using the Arkiv MCP server, repository and tutorial published
- [ ] SDK and docs issues filed

### C - DAO audit log and mainnet - 7,000 USDC

- [ ] App deployed on testnet, repository and tutorial published
- [ ] All three apps verified on mainnet within 30 days of launch, with a changelog of what had to change
- [ ] Apps and tutorials linked from the Arkiv Hub

proposals.title: golem-js examples and tutorials refresh
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

The first thing a developer does on Golem is copy an example from the docs. Today many of those examples target golem-js and yagna versions that are several releases old, and the tutorials were written before the deposits payment flow and the GPU runtime existed. A developer who hits a broken example in the first hour leaves and does not come back. Golem's own team is focused on Arkiv, so nobody is watching this rot.

This is not new features. It is making what exists work, and keeping it working with a test that runs on its own.

## What we will do

- Inventory every code example and tutorial in the Golem docs and the golem-js repository, and record which ones run on the current golem-js and yagna release
- Fix the ones that can be fixed with a small change; open an issue with a minimal reproduction for the ones that need SDK changes
- Add a runner that executes every example on a schedule against a testnet provider and publishes a status page: green, red, or skipped with the issue link
- Rewrite the three tutorials with the most traffic (first task, GPU task, payments with deposits) against the current APIs, and add one new tutorial for the deposits flow
- Send everything as pull requests to the official repositories; nothing lives only in a fork

## Requirements

- All work merged upstream or, where maintainers decline, published with the reason
- The status page and its runner are open source and can be run by anyone with a yagna requestor
- Every fixed example has a test that fails when it breaks again

## Milestones

### A - Inventory and runner - 4,500 USDC

- [ ] Public inventory of every example and tutorial with its current status and the failing output
- [ ] Runner executing all examples weekly against a testnet provider, status page live
- [ ] Issues filed upstream for every failure that needs an SDK change

### B - Fixes and tutorials - 7,500 USDC

- [ ] At least 80% of examples green on the status page, the rest linked to an open upstream issue
- [ ] Three rewritten tutorials and the deposits tutorial merged into the docs
- [ ] Handover note on how to add an example to the runner, and a named maintainer for the status page for 12 months

proposals.title: Governance records on Arkiv
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

Arkiv needs a dataset on launch day that people care about and that shows what the database is for. Golem's governance is that dataset. Octant has run more than a dozen epochs and moved thousands of ETH, and that history lives in the Octant backend and in scattered explorer links. This funding round already writes its ballots to Arkiv. Putting both there, with a page that reads only from Arkiv, makes the history tamper-evident, queryable by anyone, and a live demonstration of the product on the foundation's own data.

## What we will build

- **Importer**: reads every Octant epoch, project, allocation and matching result from the public contracts and API, and writes them to Arkiv as records with indexed attributes (epoch, project, donor, amount)
- **Round records**: the projects, sponsorships, sealed and revealed ballots and the tally of this RankedShares round, written to Arkiv by the existing ballot path and completed with the results
- **Public page**: a static site that rebuilds the whole history from Arkiv queries alone, no backend: epochs, projects over time, this round's outcome, and a query box for ad-hoc questions
- **Verification**: a script anyone can run that recomputes an epoch's allocations from the Arkiv records and compares them with the on-chain result

## Requirements

- The page has no server; every number comes from an Arkiv query in the browser
- Records are written by a wallet the community controls, and the importer is open source so anyone can re-run it and compare
- The dataset is updated within a week of each new Octant allocation window closing

## Milestones

### A - Octant history - 7,000 USDC

- [ ] Importer published and all past Octant epochs written to the Arkiv testnet
- [ ] Verification script recomputes at least three epochs and matches the on-chain result

### B - This round and the page - 6,000 USDC

- [ ] This round's projects, ballots and tally on Arkiv, readable from the records alone
- [ ] Public page live, reading only from Arkiv, with the ad-hoc query box

### C - Mainnet and upkeep - 3,000 USDC

- [ ] Dataset migrated to Arkiv mainnet within 30 days of launch
- [ ] Two subsequent Octant windows imported within a week of closing, and a handover note for the next maintainer

proposals.title: Octant analytics dashboard
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

Octant publishes results epoch by epoch, but the questions people ask cut across epochs: is GLM locking growing, which projects keep getting funded, how much of the rewards are donated rather than claimed, how concentrated are the donors. Today answering any of these means scraping the API and building a spreadsheet, and every analysis is thrown away when the next epoch closes. A maintained dashboard turns the same data into a shared reference that projects, donors and the foundation can point at.

## What we will build

- An indexer that pulls epochs, locks, rewards, allocations and matching from the Octant contracts and public API, and stores them in a small open database
- A dashboard with the core views: GLM locked and number of lockers over time; rewards claimed versus donated per epoch; funding per project across all epochs; matching ratio per project; donor concentration per epoch
- A CSV and JSON export for every view
- Automatic refresh after each allocation window closes, and on a daily schedule during a window

## Requirements

- Open source, self-hostable with one command, no paid data provider
- Every number links to the transaction or API record it comes from
- Reviewed by at least two Octant beneficiaries before the first public release

## Milestones

### A - Indexer and first views - 5,000 USDC

- [ ] Indexer published with all past epochs loaded
- [ ] Dashboard live with locks over time, claimed versus donated, and funding per project

### B - Full dashboard - 3,500 USDC

- [ ] Matching ratio and donor concentration views, CSV and JSON exports
- [ ] Reviewed by two beneficiaries, feedback published and addressed

### C - Two live windows - 1,500 USDC

- [ ] Dashboard refreshed automatically through two allocation windows without manual work
- [ ] Handover note and a named maintainer for the following 12 months

proposals.title: Yagna packaging for home nodes
proposals.body:
## Why this matters

Golem has hundreds of providers online and most of them were set up by hand from the install script, which means they drift out of date and go offline silently. Meanwhile home-server platforms like Umbrel and Start9 have tens of thousands of users who install a node with one click and never see a terminal. Golem is not in any of those catalogues. NixOS users, who run a large share of hobbyist infrastructure, have no module either.

Packaging is cheap, boring and exactly what a community can do without waiting on the core team.

## What we will do

- **NixOS module**: `services.yagna` with options for the wallet, subnet, pricing and runtimes, sent as a pull request to nixpkgs
- **Docker Compose stack**: yagna plus the provider agent and the VM runtime, with a documented way to pass through KVM and, where present, a GPU
- **Umbrel app** and **Start9 package**: install, show a QR for the wallet, show earnings and job count in the app UI, update automatically with each yagna release
- A shared setup guide covering the router and NAT configuration questions that fill the support channel

## Requirements

- Every package pins a yagna release and has a tested upgrade path to the next one
- Each package is submitted to its official catalogue; where a catalogue declines, the package is published with install instructions and the reason
- No package embeds a wallet key; the user brings or generates one on first run

## Milestones

### A - NixOS and Docker - 4,000 USDC

- [ ] NixOS module merged into nixpkgs or open as a pull request with review in progress, with a test that starts a provider in a VM
- [ ] Docker Compose stack published with the KVM and GPU passthrough guide, verified on three machines

### B - Umbrel and Start9 - 4,000 USDC

- [ ] Umbrel app submitted to the community app store with earnings and job count in the UI
- [ ] Start9 package submitted to the registry with the same screens

### C - Maintenance - 2,000 USDC

- [ ] Two yagna releases shipped through all four packages within two weeks of the upstream release
- [ ] Setup guide for router and NAT published and linked from the docs
